answers: The source problem is the one you already understand, and the target problem is the one you are trying to solve right now. Analogical transfer goes from source to target, and it succeeds when the reasoning you worked out on the source carries over to the new problem. In the example, the Russian marriage problem is the source, because its structure is easy to see, and the mutilated checkerboard is the target.

The marriages correspond to the dominoes, because each one pairs exactly one of each kind. The men and the women correspond to the two colors of squares, so the dark squares are like one group and the light squares are like the other. The two bachelors who died match the two missing corners, and the two women left without partners match the two leftover squares of one color.

Duncker's radiation problem needed you to send several low-intensity rays from different directions so they converge on the tumor at the same time. Each ray is weak enough to pass safely through healthy tissue, but where they meet their combined strength destroys the tumor. Only about 10 percent of people reached that solution without any help, which is why it makes such a good test of analogy.

That is the converging solution, which is the same idea behind the radiation problem. A strong force is needed at one target, but only weak forces can travel along any single road safely, so you split the force into small groups, send them along separate paths, and have them arrive together. Each group is harmless on its own, and the full strength exists only at the fortress.

Without any story, about 10 percent solved radiation. After reading the fortress story, about 30 percent solved it, which is three times better but still leaves most people stuck. When they were then told to think about the story they had read, the rate jumped to about 75 percent. So the knowledge was in their heads; what was missing was noticing that it applied.

answers.topic: Noticing, surface similarity, and structural correspondence
answers: It showed that a source with similar surface features gets noticed and used. Of the people who knew the radiation problem, 81 percent solved the lightbulb problem, compared with only 10 percent of a control group with no source. Rays and lasers, tumors and filaments, and tissue and glass look alike, so the link comes to mind easily. That is far better than the fortress story managed, which helped only about 30 percent.

Surface features are the particular objects and details in a problem, like a fortress, a tumor, a laser, or a filament. They are what the problem looks like. Structural features are the underlying principle that governs the solution, the reason the solution works. In radiation and the lightbulb, the structure is that a strong beam would harm what surrounds the target, so the beam has to be split.

Because the fragile-glass version shares the reason for using several weak beams. In both problems a strong beam would damage the surroundings, the glass or the healthy tissue, so the structure matches, and 69 percent solved radiation. In the insufficient-intensity version the glass is never at risk; the lasers were just too weak, so readers had the steps without the principle, and only 33 percent solved it. Structure mattered more than surface.

Analogical encoding is comparing two problems or stories and working out what they have in common. It is an effective way to get people to pay attention to structural features. When you compare, say, a soldier story and a laser story, the details that belong to only one of them fade, and the shared idea of weak forces combining at a target stands out. Then you can recognize it in a problem that looks completely different.

That is mapping. Noticing is recognizing that a source problem might be relevant at all, and applying is using the mapping to build a concrete solution. Connecting the central target to the separate approaches means lining up the parts of the source with the parts of the target, like the fortress with the tumor and the small groups with the weak rays, so it is the mapping step.

The analogical paradox is that analogies are hard to apply in the laboratory, yet people use them all the time in real settings. People miss a useful source in an experiment when they are handed an unfamiliar story, but in their own work they come up with analogies from knowledge they understand well. Those analogies tend to share both surface and structural features with the problem, so they are easy to notice and use.

Scientists use about 3 to 15 analogies in a one-hour lab meeting. That shows analogies are common in real work even though people often miss them in lab tasks. They draw on deep knowledge of related experiments, so their analogies fit the problem in both surface and structure, which is part of why they come to mind so readily.

In vivo problem-solving research studies problem solving where it naturally happens. People are observed to see how they actually solve problems in the real world, such as scientists in their own lab meetings. In vivo means in the living, meaning real life as opposed to the lab. Its advantage is the naturalistic setting, which shows how people really solve problems at work.

One tradeoff is that researchers cannot isolate and control variables the way they can in an experiment. You get real context, but you lose the control that lets you say what caused what. It is also time-consuming. So you gain a naturalistic setting and give up the tight control of the lab.

answers.topic: Expert knowledge, chunks, and problem organization
answers: Chase and Simon (1973) compared a chess master with a beginner who had under 100 hours of play. After seeing a board for five seconds, the master reproduced real game positions far better, because those positions were stored in long-term memory and accessed in chunks. With random arrangements, those chunks were not available, so the master's advantage mostly vanished. The expert's edge is organized knowledge, not a general memory advantage.

A chunk is a group of pieces that forms a familiar pattern from real games and is stored in long-term memory. An expert sees a position as a few meaningful chunks instead of many separate pieces, so five seconds is enough to recall it. A beginner has few stored patterns and has to remember each piece on its own.

Chi and colleagues (1982) gave 24 physics problems to experts, who were physics professors, and to novices, who were students with one semester of physics, and asked them to sort the problems by similarity. Novices sorted by surface features, what the objects looked like, so blocks on slopes went together. Experts sorted by structural features, the underlying principles, so problems needing conservation of energy went together even when they looked different.

The expert is using structural features, in particular the underlying physics principle, here conservation of energy. Problem 21 is a compressed spring pushing a block along a flat surface, with no slope, so it looks nothing like problem 24. But both are solved with conservation of energy, and the expert files problems under the principle that solves them. A novice would pair 24 with 23 because both have inclined planes.

No. Experts are no better than novices when given problems outside their field, because expertise belongs to a particular domain. A chess master has no special edge in physics, and a physicist has none in chess. The advantage comes from knowledge of the field, organized in long-term memory, and not from some general problem-solving ability.

answers.topic: Creativity, divergent thinking, and implementing solutions
answers: Divergent thinking is open-ended thinking that produces a large number of potential solutions. Instead of narrowing straight to one answer, you generate many possible answers to one question, which raises the odds that one of them turns out to be good. It is a key part of creativity, along with novel ideas and new connections between existing ideas.

After ideas are generated, they still have to be evaluated, planned, and implemented. Creative problem solving is a process with stages: problem finding and fact finding, then problem definition and idea finding, then evaluation and planning, and finally solution implementation, which means taking action. Ideas are necessary, but having an idea and producing a solution are two different achievements.

Too much knowledge can hinder creativity because problems often need flexible thinking and the rejection of accepted procedures. Someone who knows the usual approach very well may struggle to set it aside, much like the danger experts face. Knowledge gives the raw material for ideas, but it also supplies familiar procedures that can crowd out new approaches.

It requires being willing to reject the usual procedure and use another one that is used less often. A well-practiced method tends to come to mind first and can work like a mental set, blocking alternatives. So when a problem calls for an unusual approach, you have to drop the familiar method, and the same deep knowledge that makes experts fast can make them rigid.

Decisions are the process of making choices between alternatives, while reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions. They are closely linked, because decisions are based on the judgments we make, and reaching those judgments involves reasoning. For example, judging that rain is likely is reasoning, and deciding to bring an umbrella is the decision that follows from it.

Inductive reasoning is reasoning based on observations. You reach conclusions from evidence by going from particular cases to a general conclusion. It is one of the primary mechanisms behind judgments, and it is the basis of scientific investigations, where observations are made, data are collected, and conclusions are drawn. We also use it in everyday life to predict the future from past experience.

The strength of an inductive argument depends on three things. First is how representative the observations are of the whole category. Second is how many observations there are, since more give stronger support. Third is the quality of the observations, because careful, accurate ones count for more. Sometimes one very compelling, high-quality observation can carry a great deal of weight.

Many white swans support the claim that all swans are white, but one clearly observed black swan contradicts it. An inductive conclusion is a general claim built from particular cases, so a single clear counterexample can prove it false no matter how many cases supported it before. That is how much one high-quality observation can weigh.

Because the conclusions go beyond the observations we have, and a new observation can always overturn them. In induction, conclusions are probably, but not definitely, true, and they are suggested with various degrees of certainty. They are always open to revision, unlike a conclusion that must follow from its premises.

About 70 percent of people said more words begin with r, but in reality three times more words have r in the third position. That is the availability heuristic. Words starting with r are easy to retrieve, because memory lets us search by first letter, while third-letter words are hard to retrieve even though there are far more of them. People answer by ease of recall, not by true frequency.

Base-rate neglect is ignoring how common each category is in the population when a description is available. In the Jack problem, a group has 70 lawyers and 30 engineers. With no description, people correctly say the chance of an engineer is 30 percent. But once Jack is described as careful, conservative, and fond of carpentry and math puzzles, people say engineer, even though the group still has far more lawyers.

Because feminist bank tellers are a smaller group inside the group of all bank tellers, so the combination cannot be more probable than one part alone. This is the conjunction rule. About 82 percent picked the feminist option, since it sounds more like Linda. That sense of fit overrides the logic, which is representativeness producing an error.

The correct answer is the smaller hospital, with about 15 births a day. Sample size controls how far a percentage can drift from the true value by chance. With few births, the share of boys swings widely, so days over 60 percent boys happen more often, while the larger hospital stays nearer 50 percent. Yet 56 percent said about the same, and only 22 percent chose the smaller hospital.

The law of large numbers says that the larger the number of individuals randomly drawn from a population, the more representative the resulting group will be of the whole population. A large sample evens out chance variation, while a small one can be thrown off by a few unusual cases. People wrongly expect small samples to look representative, which is the error in the hospital problem.

answers.topic: Illusory correlation, myside bias, and hypothesis testing
answers: An illusory correlation is when a correlation appears to exist, but either does not exist or is much weaker than assumed. It tends to happen when we expect two things to be related, so what we expect guides what we notice, and what we notice guides what we believe. We fool ourselves into thinking they are related even when they are not.

A stereotype leads people to pay particular attention to behaviors associated with that stereotype. That selective attention makes those behaviors more available in memory, so they come to mind easily. People then take those easily recalled examples as proof of the stereotype, creating an illusory correlation that reinforces it. They notice the cases that fit and miss the many that do not.

Lord and colleagues (1979) had people in favor of capital punishment and people against it read the same article, which presented evidence for both sides. Each group found that the article supported its own view. The identical information strengthened opposite beliefs, so the difference came entirely from how each group judged it. This is the myside bias, favoring evidence that agrees with your own opinions.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for information that fits a hypothesis and overlook information that argues against it. Myside bias is a type of confirmation bias, specifically generating and evaluating evidence and testing hypotheses in a way biased toward your own opinions and attitudes. So the 2, 4, 6 task shows confirmation bias in general, while the capital punishment article shows myside bias.

The actual rule was three numbers in increasing order of magnitude, so any rising sequence fit. The most common hypothesis was increasing intervals of two. People kept testing sets that matched their own guess, and every such set also fit the real rule, so the yes feedback made them confident in the wrong rule. Only a set that breaks your own guess could reveal that the real rule is broader.

answers.topic: Utility, probabilities, and choices that cause harm
answers: Expected utility theory assumes that people are rational. If they have all the relevant information, they will make the decision that results in the maximum expected utility, which combines how good each outcome is with how likely it is. In its early form, utility meant maximum monetary payoff. You multiply each outcome's value by its probability, add them up, and choose the largest total.

Because utility is not necessarily money, and people find value in other things, like safety, fairness, or how a choice makes them feel. Many decisions do not maximize the probability of the best outcome. People gamble in casinos all the time, even though they know the odds are very much against them. So the approach is a strong standard but a weak description of how people really choose.

Most people chose the bowl with 7 red jellybeans out of 100. But the other bowl, with 1 red out of 10, has the higher probability, 10 percent compared with 7 percent. Their choice was influenced by considerations other than probability. The second bowl has more red beans, so it seems to offer more chances, but people should compare ratios, not counts.

Ritov and Baron (1999) asked about a food convoy that could be rerouted to a second camp, saving 1,000 people but causing 100 in the first camp to die. Rerouting saves 900 more lives, so expected utility says to reroute, yet 63 percent did not. Twelve percent would not change the route even if only one person in the first camp would die. Causing harm by acting weighed more than the larger benefit.

After the September 11 attacks, air travel decreased and driving increased, even though the probability of dying in a car accident is far greater than dying in a plane. More Americans lost their lives on the road than the total number of passengers killed on the four hijacked flights. The choice that felt safer was actually more dangerous. Fear and vivid, heavily reported events made flying feel riskier than it was.

answers.topic: Sacred values, taboo and tragic tradeoffs
answers: A sacred value is something people treat as beyond price, such as human life, loyalty, or justice, and people want to protect it. In the sacred value protection model of Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, and Lerner (2000), sacred values are kept in a separate compartment from secular values like money and time. When the two are mixed together, people feel threatened and respond with moral outrage.

A taboo tradeoff mixes the sacred and secular domains, such as trading a child's life for money, and it provokes moral outrage because putting a price on something sacred treats it as a commodity. A tragic tradeoff compares two sacred values with each other, such as choosing between two lives. It is painful, but people are less morally outraged because the choice does not cross the line between sacred and secular.

Tetlock and colleagues (2000) had a hospital administrator decide whether to save Johnny, a boy needing a liver transplant. In the taboo scenario, his life was weighed against a million dollars. Not saving him produced very high outrage, about 5.4 on a scale topping out at 6, compared with about 2.5 when he was saved. So the choice mattered a great deal when a life was traded for money.

The tragic tradeoff, where one child's life was set against another's because there was only one liver. Outrage was moderate and nearly the same whether or not Johnny was saved. Either way a life was saved, so neither option broke the line between sacred and secular. Outcome matters less when two sacred values are compared.

The participants were Israeli settlers, 601 of them, Palestinian refugees, 535, and Palestinian students affiliated with various political groups, 719. All were directly involved in the Israeli and Palestinian conflict, so the study extended the earlier findings from imagined scenarios to a realistic setting with real stakes. They were offered deals as possible solutions to the conflict.

Taboo+ added money to the taboo compromise: Israel would pay Palestine 1 billion dollars a year for 10 years. The symbolic version added a symbolic concession instead. Israel would recognize the historic and legitimate right of the Palestinians to their own state and apologize for the wrongs done to them. Recognition and an apology address what the other side holds sacred, so the deal becomes a tragic tradeoff.

They responded in opposite ways. For non-absolutists, adding money slightly lowered anger and disgust and lowered support for violence, just as a cost and benefit view predicts. For moral absolutists, adding money raised anger and disgust and raised support for violence. For them, money turned a hard compromise into an insulting trade of the sacred for cash. They judge a deal by what it says about their values, not its payoff.

Among the settlers, 46 percent were moral absolutists. They believed it was never permissible for the Jewish people to give up part of the Land of Israel, no matter how great the benefit. For Palestinian students, the figure was 54 percent, who treated both the right of return and Jerusalem as sacred values.

Symbolic recognition did better than money. Adding recognition and an apology lowered anger and disgust and also lowered support for violence, so a symbolic gesture succeeded where money failed. For moral absolutists, money raised anger and support for violence. When a value is sacred, material incentives backfire, while a symbolic concession answers a sacred value with a sacred value, which feels less like a betrayal.

answers.topic: Nuclear-program study, manipulations, measures, and energy results
answers: It was an online study conducted in Farsi with 1,997 Iranian participants, using a 2 by 3 design. One factor was the nuclear program, energy or weapons, and the other was the type of deal, Taboo, Taboo+, or Taboo-. This was by Dehghani, Atran, and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev, and colleagues (2009). It asked whether Iranians who hold the program as sacred would be open to material incentives or disincentives.

In the Taboo deal, Iran gives up its program and surrenders its nuclear facilities to the UN, and in return Israel does the same. Taboo+ adds an incentive, 40 billion dollars in economic funds from the United Nations to Iran. Taboo- adds a disincentive instead, so that if Iran does not accept the deal, the UN would impose additional sanctions. Incentives change the benefit of accepting, and disincentives change the cost of refusing.

Participants were asked what they thought about Iran giving up its program. Those who chose the final answer, that it should not be done no matter how great the consequences, were classified as holding a sacred value. That refuses every tradeoff, whatever is offered. It was 14 percent of participants for nuclear energy and 13 percent for nuclear weapons.

For sacred-value participants in the energy condition, approval was lower than for the others, and adding funds or sanctions lowered it even further. Anger was higher, and adding money or sanctions raised it, with anger highest with funds. So sweeteners and threats made the deal less acceptable. Participants without a sacred value approved highly and expected little anger, because to them money and sanctions are ordinary costs and benefits.

Participants gave three judgments about each deal. They rated their own personal approval of the deal, how angry people would be if the Iranian government approved it, and whether they would find the deal misleading if it were really proposed to Iran. Approval measured personal support, anger measured the expected public reaction, and the misleading question asked about distrust of the deal's intentions.
